## Learning objectives
\Large
By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

* Explain why we split data into training and test sets
* Compute overall accuracy and explain when it misleads
* Build and read a confusion matrix
* Define sensitivity, specificity, and related metrics
* Build and evaluate a gene-expression biomarker for TB: cutoff, ROC curve, AUC
* Explain how prevalence changes predictive values
* Choose a metric that fits the biomedical question

## Evaluation metrics
\Large
Before optimizing algorithms, we need to define what "better" means. We use `caret` and the `heights` data from dslabs.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
library(dslabs)
data(heights)
```

## Evaluation metrics
\Large
Height by sex:
```{r,out.width="50%", fig.align="center"}
boxplot(heights$height~heights$sex)
```

## Evaluation metrics
\Large
Simple example: predict sex from height.

```{r}
y <- heights$sex
x <- heights$height
```

## Evaluation metrics
\Large
* One predictor (height) and a categorical outcome (`Male`/`Female`)
* Heights overlap a lot, so we won't predict $Y$ very accurately
* Can we beat guessing? We need a quantitative definition of "better"

## Training and test sets {#training-test}
\Large
Algorithms are judged on new data. So we split the data:

* __Training set:__ outcomes known; used to build the algorithm
* __Test set:__ we pretend outcomes are unknown; used only to evaluate

## Training and test sets
\Large
`caret::createDataPartition` randomly splits the data:

```{r}
set.seed(2007)
test_index <- createDataPartition(y, times = 1, 
                                  p = 0.5, list = FALSE)
```

`times`: number of splits; `p`: proportion in the index; `list`: return a list or not.


## Training and test sets
\Large 
Define the two sets:

```{r}
test_set <- heights[test_index, ]
train_set <- heights[-test_index, ]
```

Develop using **only** the training set, then __freeze__ the algorithm and evaluate it on the test set. The simplest metric is __overall accuracy__.

## Overall accuracy
\Large
The simplest possible algorithm: guess.

```{r}
y_hat <- sample(c("Male", "Female"), 
                length(test_index), replace = TRUE)
```

This ignores height entirely.

## Overall accuracy
\Large
ML functions in R usually expect categorical outcomes as factors:

```{r}
y_hat <- sample(c("Male", "Female"), 
                length(test_index), replace = TRUE) %>%
  factor(levels = levels(test_set$sex))
```

## Overall accuracy
\Large
_Overall accuracy_ is the proportion predicted correctly:

```{r}
mean(y_hat == test_set$sex)
```

About 50%. We are guessing!

## Overall accuracy
\Large
Can we do better? On average, males are slightly taller:

```{r}
heights %>% group_by(sex) %>% 
  summarize(mean(height), sd(height))
```

## Overall accuracy
\Large
Another simple rule: predict `Male` if height is above 62 inches (about two SDs below the average male):

```{r}
y_hat <- ifelse(x > 62, "Male", "Female") %>% 
  factor(levels = levels(test_set$sex))
```

Accuracy goes from 0.50 to about 0.80:

```{r}
mean(y == y_hat)
```

## Overall accuracy
\Large
Can we pick a better cutoff than 62? Try several and keep the best.

**Optimize the cutoff on the training set only**: the test set is only for evaluation.

## Overall accuracy
Training-set accuracy for 10 cutoffs:

```{r}
cutoff <- seq(61, 70)
accuracy <- map_dbl(cutoff, function(x){
  y_hat <- ifelse(train_set$height > x, "Male", "Female") %>% 
    factor(levels = levels(test_set$sex))
  mean(y_hat == train_set$sex)
})
```

## Overall accuracy
Training-set accuracy by cutoff:

```{r accuracy-vs-cutoff, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center"}
data.frame(cutoff, accuracy) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(cutoff, accuracy)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() 
```

## Overall accuracy
\Large The maximum accuracy:

```{r}
max(accuracy)
```

and its cutoff:

```{r}
best_cutoff <- cutoff[which.max(accuracy)]
best_cutoff
```

## Overall accuracy
\Large
Check this cutoff on the test set, so the estimate isn't over-optimistic:

```{r}
y_hat <- ifelse(test_set$height > 
  best_cutoff,"Male","Female") %>% 
  factor(levels = levels(test_set$sex))
mean(y_hat == test_set$sex)
```

## The confusion matrix
\Large
Overall accuracy can be deceptive. The _confusion matrix_ tabulates predictions against truth:

```{r}
table(predicted = y_hat, actual = test_set$sex)
```

## The confusion matrix
Accuracy computed separately by sex reveals a problem:

```{r}
test_set %>% 
  mutate(y_hat = y_hat) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>% 
  summarize(accuracy = mean(y_hat == sex))
```

## The confusion matrix
\Large
Too many females are predicted male, because the __prevalence__ of males is high:

```{r}
prev <- mean(y == "Male")
prev
```

## The confusion matrix
\Large
In overall accuracy, the many errors for females are outweighed by correct calls for males. **This is a big problem in machine learning.**


## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large
The four entries of the __confusion matrix__:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
mat <- matrix(c("True positives (TP)", "False negatives (FN)", 
                "False positives (FP)", "True negatives (TN)"), 2, 2)
colnames(mat) <- c("Actually Positive", "Actually Negative")
rownames(mat) <- c("Predicted positive", "Predicted negative")
tmp <- as.data.frame(mat)
if(knitr::is_html_output()){
  knitr::kable(tmp, "html") %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE)
} else{
  knitr::kable(tmp, "latex", booktabs = TRUE) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 8)
}
```

## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large
**Sensitivity** = $TP/(TP+FN)$: the proportion of actual positives called positive.

Also called the __true positive rate__ (TPR) or __recall__.

## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large
**Specificity** = $TN/(TN+FP)$: the proportion of actual negatives called negative.

Also called the __true negative rate__ (TNR).

## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large
**Precision** = $TP/(TP+FP)$: the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive.

Also called __positive predictive value__ (PPV). Unlike TPR and TNR, precision depends on prevalence: higher prevalence gives higher precision even when guessing.


## Sensitivity and specificity 
Summary of the terms:


| Measure of | Name 1 | Name 2 | Definition | Probability representation |
|---------|-----|----------|--------|------------------|
sensitivity | TPR | Recall | $\frac{\mbox{TP}}{\mbox{TP} + \mbox{FN}}$ | $\mbox{Pr}(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1)$ |
specificity | TNR | 1-FPR | $\frac{\mbox{TN}}{\mbox{TN}+\mbox{FP}}$ | $\mbox{Pr}(\hat{Y}=0 \mid Y=0)$ |
Precision |  PPV |  | $\frac{\mbox{TP}}{\mbox{TP}+\mbox{FP}}$ | $\mbox{Pr}(Y=1 \mid \hat{Y}=1)$|

Here TPR is True Positive Rate, FPR is False Positive Rate, and PPV is Positive Predictive Value.

## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large
`caret::confusionMatrix` computes all of these. It expects factors and treats the **first level** as positive ($Y=1$); here that is `Female` (alphabetical).

```{r}
cm <- confusionMatrix(data = y_hat, 
                      reference = test_set$sex)
```

## Sensitivity and specificity 
Access the metrics directly:

```{r}
cm$overall["Accuracy"]
cm$byClass[c("Sensitivity","Specificity", "Prevalence")]
```

## Sensitivity and specificity 
\Large

Overall accuracy is high despite low sensitivity, because female prevalence is low (0.23).

Missing females (low sensitivity) costs less accuracy than missing males would (low specificity).


## Application: a blood biomarker for tuberculosis
\Large
**Biomarker development:** find a measurable signal that predicts disease, then prove it works in new patients.

* Discovery: which genes differ between active TB and latent infection (LTBI)?
* Signature: combine a few genes into one **score**
* Threshold: pick a cutoff for the intended use
* Validation: test it on samples not used to build it

## The TB NanoString data
\large
Blood gene expression for 107 TB-related genes in 179 people with active TB or latent TB infection (Kaipilyawar et al., *Clin Infect Dis*, 2022):

\normalsize
```{r tb-data, message=FALSE}
tb <- readRDS("TBnanostring.rds")
tb$TB_Status <- factor(tb$TB_Status, levels = c("LTBI", "TB"))
dim(tb)
table(tb$TB_Status)
```

## A three-gene signature
\large
Sweeney et al. (2016) found a 3-gene score that separates active TB from other conditions: $(\text{GBP5} + \text{DUSP3})/2 - \text{KLF2}$. All three genes are on the panel:

\normalsize
```{r tb-score, out.width="40%", fig.width=4.5, fig.height=3.5, fig.align='center'}
tb$score <- (tb$GBP5 + tb$DUSP3) / 2 - tb$KLF2
boxplot(score ~ TB_Status, data = tb, ylab = "Sweeney3 score")
```

## Choosing a cutoff
\large
Every cutoff gives a different sensitivity and specificity. The **intended use** decides which matters most.

* WHO target for a TB **triage** test: sensitivity $\ge$ 90%, specificity $\ge$ 70%
* Missing active TB is worse than a false alarm (which gets a confirmatory test)

\normalsize
```{r tb-cut}
set.seed(1)
idx <- createDataPartition(tb$TB_Status, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
tb_train <- tb[idx, ]; tb_test <- tb[-idx, ]
# cutoff that catches 90% of TB cases in the training set
cut <- quantile(tb_train$score[tb_train$TB_Status == "TB"], 0.10)
```

## Evaluating on the test set
\small
```{r tb-cm}
pred <- factor(ifelse(tb_test$score > cut, "TB", "LTBI"),
               levels = c("LTBI", "TB"))
cm_tb <- confusionMatrix(pred, tb_test$TB_Status, positive = "TB")
cm_tb$table
round(cm_tb$byClass[c("Sensitivity", "Specificity",
                      "Pos Pred Value", "Neg Pred Value")], 3)
```

\normalsize
Test sensitivity is a bit below the 90% we aimed for: with only `r sum(tb_test$TB_Status == "TB")` TB cases in the test set, estimates are noisy. (Cross-validation helps; next lecture.)

## ROC curves and AUC
\Large
* The **ROC curve** plots sensitivity vs. 1 $-$ specificity across **all** cutoffs
* The **area under the curve (AUC)**: probability that a random TB case scores higher than a random LTBI case
* AUC = 0.5 is a coin flip; AUC = 1 is perfect
* AUC summarizes the score; the cutoff is a separate decision

## ROC curve for the TB score
\small
```{r tb-roc, fig.show='hide', message=FALSE}
library(pROC)
roc_tb <- roc(tb_test$TB_Status, tb_test$score, levels = c("LTBI", "TB"),
              direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_tb, print.auc = TRUE, legacy.axes = TRUE)
```

## ROC curve for the TB score
```{r tb-roc-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="42%", fig.width=4.5, fig.height=4.5, fig.align='center'}
plot(roc_tb, print.auc = TRUE, legacy.axes = TRUE)
```

## Prevalence changes predictive values
\large
Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test. **PPV** and **NPV** also depend on how common TB is in the people tested:

\normalsize
```{r tb-ppv}
sens <- unname(cm_tb$byClass["Sensitivity"])
spec <- unname(cm_tb$byClass["Specificity"])
ppv <- function(prev)
  sens * prev / (sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev))
round(c(`study (44%)` = ppv(0.44), `clinic (10%)` = ppv(0.10),
        `screening (1%)` = ppv(0.01)), 3)
```

\normalsize
At 1% prevalence, most positives are false alarms: a triage test needs a confirmatory test.

## Summary
\large
* Always evaluate on data the model has not seen
* Overall accuracy can hide poor performance when classes are imbalanced
* The confusion matrix underlies every classification metric
* Sensitivity and specificity trade off as the cutoff changes
* ROC/AUC summarize a biomarker score; the cutoff depends on the intended use
* PPV and NPV depend on prevalence: a great test can still give mostly false positives in screening
* Pick metrics by the cost of each type of error (e.g., missed TB case vs. false alarm)
